GLEUHR
Front Desk Function  •  The Receptionist
Aesthetic Medicine
Reception Playbook
Version 1.0   |   The First Impression, the Last Impression, and Every Moment Between
A reception is not a desk.
It is the first face a patient sees when she has spent weeks deciding to walk through that door,
and the last voice she hears as she leaves carrying a story she will tell someone tonight.

This playbook is about how you hold both ends of that day.


The Receptionist's Inner Stance
Read this before the doors open. It takes a minute. It is the difference between a desk that runs the day and a desk that runs the brand.
What the patient is actually carrying
The woman walking toward your door has been thinking about this visit for weeks. She rehearsed how she will describe her skin to a stranger. She checked the location three times. She arrived ten minutes early and sat in the car for five of them because she did not want to look anxious walking in. She is wondering whether the people inside will be kind, whether she will be judged, whether the place will feel expensive and cold, whether she will be one of fifty patients today and made to feel it.
She does not arrive at your desk asking these questions out loud. She arrives looking for the answers in your face.
The desk-job trap
Receptionists are often hired to manage tasks — phones, forms, appointments, payments. That is the job description. It is not the job.
The real job is that you are the first human face of GLEUHR. Every patient who ever becomes a long-term client, every referral that ever comes through our door, every five-star review we ever get — has passed through you twice. Once on the way in, and once on the way out. The doctor inside is the reason she came. You are the reason she stayed.
INNER STANCE  Your phone is the patient's enemy at your desk. The need to finish what you are typing = the patient feeling unimportant. The need to keep eyes on the screen = the patient feeling unseen. The need to look busy = the patient feeling like an intrusion. Look up. Stand briefly. Smile. The work on your screen can wait twenty seconds. The patient who walked in cannot.
Your three jobs at this desk
1.  Make her feel welcomed. Within the first five seconds of her walking in, she should feel that someone was waiting for her.
2.  Make her feel expected. Use her name. Refer to her appointment. Reassure her that the team inside knows she is here.
3.  Make her feel calm. Whatever happens behind the scenes — a doctor running late, a system that is slow, a colleague who is irritable — the patient on the other side of your desk should feel none of it. Your face is the weather of the clinic.
The receptionist you should be
Picture the most graceful person you know at hosting people in her home. The one who notices when a guest is uncomfortable, who remembers who likes tea and who likes water, who never makes anyone feel like they came at a bad time — even when they did. That is the energy of this desk. Calm. Warm. Quietly attentive. Never harried, never bored. Genuinely glad each person walked in.
That is the receptionist your patient came here to meet. Be that receptionist.
0.  Before the Doors Open
The fifteen minutes before the first patient changes the entire day.
Check today's appointment list. Read each patient's name. Note who is new, who is returning, who is here for a sensitive treatment. A name read once in the morning lands when she walks in.
Wipe the desk. Straighten the brochures. Refill the water. The patient who sees a clean, ordered desk reads it as: this place takes care of details.
Check that the seating area is set. Cushions placed, magazines current, lights warm not harsh, music soft, fragrance subtle, washroom clean.
Brief yourself silently on anything unusual today — a VIP, a complaint follow-up, a doctor running late, a counsellor on leave. Surprises at the desk become friction for the patient.
Take a breath. Whatever is happening in your life right now stays on this side of the desk.
AVOID  Do not be on your phone when the first patient walks in. Do not be eating at the desk — ever. Do not have headphones in. Do not have a colleague leaning over the desk in personal conversation. The first impression is being formed before she even says hello.
1.  The Phone Enquiry  —  The First Contact, Often Ever
The moment
A woman has decided, after months of thinking, to dial our number. She has not committed to anything yet — she is testing the temperature of this place by your voice. If you sound rushed, she will hang up and never call back, and neither of us will ever know we lost her.
Pick up by the third ring
Stop whatever you are doing. The phone is the patient. The phone is more important than the form you are filling, the colleague you are talking to, the WhatsApp on your screen.
What you say
“Good morning, GLEUHR Wellness, [your name] speaking. How can I help you today?”
Slow that line down. Most clinics rush it. Yours should sound unhurried — because every word the caller hears is being read for warmth.
If she is asking about a treatment or price
The instinct is to quote a number. Resist it. A number on a phone call to a stranger means very little; what you want is to invite her in for a consultation, where the doctor can actually see her skin.
“That's a great question — and the honest answer is that the treatment really depends on what your skin needs, and that's something our doctor will assess in your first consultation. Would you like me to book you in? The consultation itself is short, and you'll leave knowing exactly what your skin needs and what it would involve.”
If she is hesitant, says she'll think about it
“Of course — take your time. May I take your name and a number so I can hold a slot for you for the next week? No commitment — it just means when you decide, you won't have to wait for a date. And if you have any questions before then, please feel free to call me back directly — my name is [your name].”
THE PSYCHOLOGY  The caller's biggest fear is being added to a pushy follow-up list. By offering to hold a slot rather than book one, and by giving her your name so the next call has a person attached to it, you turn the enquiry from a transaction into a small relationship. Most callers who feel that way call back. Almost no caller who feels chased does.
Closing the call
“Thank you for calling — we'll see you on [date] at [time]. If anything changes before then, just message us on this number. Have a lovely day.”
AVOID  Do not say "madam" repeatedly — it sounds rehearsed. Do not say "please hold" without asking first. Do not transfer a caller more than once. Do not put a caller on hold and forget her on the line — if it takes more than 30 seconds, come back to her: "sorry to keep you waiting, just one more moment."
2.  The Walk-in Welcome  —  The First Eight Seconds
The moment
She has just pushed open the glass door. Her eyes are scanning — looking for someone to make eye contact with, looking for confirmation that she is in the right place, looking to see whether this is somewhere she belongs. Eight seconds. That is your window.
What you do
Look up immediately. Even if you are mid-typing, mid-call, mid-anything — look up.
Smile. Not the customer-service smile. The smile you give when someone you were expecting arrives.
Stand briefly, or rise slightly out of your chair. This single small movement signals welcome more than any sentence can.
Move toward her if she lingers at the door.
What you say
“Hi, welcome to GLEUHR. Please come in. Have you been with us before, or is this your first visit?”
That one sentence does three things. It welcomes her, it offers her a path forward, and it lets her tell you whether she is new (and therefore needs more orientation) or returning (and therefore needs to feel remembered). You learn what you need to know without making her feel like she has been processed.
FIRST AFFIRMATION  ·  THE WELCOME
“Welcome to GLEUHR. Please come in.”
THE PSYCHOLOGY  Patients have been conditioned by years of medical waiting rooms to expect a glass partition, an irritable face, and a number to take. When you break that expectation in the first five seconds — by being on her side of the desk, in her eye-line, glad to see her — every single thing that happens later in the visit lands more softly. The thirty seconds you spend on her welcome saves you fifteen minutes of de-escalation later.
AVOID  Do not say "name?" as your first word. Do not point to the form before saying hello. Do not stay seated behind the desk for a first-time patient — it is a barrier, and she feels it. Do not ask "do you have an appointment?" in a tone that implies she might not. Of course she has an appointment — your tone should assume it.
3.  The Returning Patient  —  Make Her Feel Remembered
There is no patient more loyal than the one who walks back in and is greeted as someone we know. There is no patient more easily lost than the one who returns and feels like a stranger.
Before her appointment
Glance at her last visit notes when you saw her name on this morning's list. Note her treatment, the doctor she saw, anything she mentioned. You will not remember every detail — but you should remember one.
What you say
“Hi [Name]ji, lovely to see you again. How have you been? Last time you were here with Dr [name] — you're with her again today.”
That is the line. "Lovely to see you again." "Last time you were here with Dr X." Two sentences that tell her: we know who you are, we kept track, we were expecting you.
THE PSYCHOLOGY  Memory is the highest form of respect. The patient who is remembered tells everyone. The patient who has to re-introduce herself to the same desk three visits in a row quietly goes elsewhere and never tells you why. This is the cheapest, highest-leverage moment in the whole patient journey — it costs you thirty seconds of preparation and earns a lifetime of loyalty.
If you do not remember
Do not pretend. The patient can tell. Recover with grace:
“Forgive me — give me one second to pull up your file so I can welcome you properly. There we go — yes, you were with Dr [name] last time. Welcome back, [Name]ji.”
4.  The New Patient  —  The Form, the Nerves, the First Walk Down the Corridor
The moment
She is here for the first time. She does not know where the washroom is, how long the wait will be, whether she will be charged before or after, what the doctor will be like, whether to keep her bag with her or leave it. She is operating on incomplete information and her nervous system knows it.
What you say after her hello
“First time with us — welcome. Let me walk you through how today will go so there are no surprises. First, I'll have you fill out a short form — just basic details, takes about three minutes. Then you'll meet our doctor for the consultation, which is unhurried. After that, our counsellor will sit with you to plan whatever the doctor has recommended. The washroom is just there if you need it, and please help yourself to water. Any questions before we start?”
THE PSYCHOLOGY  Uncertainty is the single biggest source of anxiety in a waiting room. A patient who knows exactly what is about to happen — even when what is about to happen is a clinical consultation — is calmer than a patient who is being asked to trust the unknown. Forty-five seconds of orientation at the desk saves the doctor five minutes of warming her up inside.
Handing her the form
“Just take your time with this. There's no rush. If anything is unclear, mark it and I'll help you finish it. You don't need to fill in things you're not sure about — the doctor will go through any of it with you.”
AVOID  Do not hover while she fills the form. Do not check on her every minute. Do not stare at her writing. Step back, give her privacy, glance up only to check if she has finished. Patients have shared with me that the worst part of a first visit is the feeling of being watched while filling forms. Don't be that desk.
5.  The Wait  —  The Most Emotionally Fragile Time
The moment
She has handed in the form, sat down, and now she waits. This is when the doubts return. "Why am I here. Maybe my skin is not that bad. Maybe this is going to be expensive. Maybe the doctor will judge me." Five minutes of silence in a waiting room is longer than fifteen minutes of conversation.
What you do
After two or three minutes, glance up and offer water, tea, or a brochure. Not as a script — as a host.
Walk past her seating area if you have to take something inside. The presence of a calm staff member moving through is itself reassuring.
If the doctor is genuinely running late, tell her. Do not let her wonder. "The doctor is just finishing with the patient before you — it'll be about ten more minutes. Are you okay for water?" That sentence alone resets the clock in her head.
What you say if she's been waiting more than 15 minutes
“[Name]ji, thank you so much for your patience. The doctor is wrapping up — she'll be with you in just a few more minutes. Can I get you something — tea, water, anything?”
SECOND AFFIRMATION  ·  THE WAIT
“Thank you so much for your patience. She'll be with you in just a few minutes.”
THE PSYCHOLOGY  The patient's irritation during a wait is almost never about the time. It is about feeling forgotten. A single sentence acknowledging the wait — even if the wait does not get any shorter — resets the entire emotional state. The patient who has been seen during the wait will tolerate twice the wait of one who has been ignored.
AVOID  Do not let a patient sit for twenty minutes without acknowledgement. Do not say "five more minutes" if you know it will be twenty — the lie is worse than the wait. Do not be visibly chatting with colleagues while a patient is waiting alone.
6.  The Nervous Patient  —  Reading the Body Language
Some patients announce their nervousness; most do not. You will spot it in the small things — the bag clutched on the lap, the phone scrolled without reading, the foot tapping, the eyes that drift to the door. Your job is not to ask her if she is nervous. It is to behave in a way that makes her less so.
What you do
Catch her eye. Smile gently. Do not stare — just acknowledge.
Walk over with water, even if she did not ask. "Just bringing you a glass — hydration helps for the consultation."
Lower the energy around her. If a colleague is loud nearby, redirect them quietly.
If she opens up at the desk
Sometimes a nervous patient will say something at the desk that she has not told anyone. "I've never done anything like this before." "I've been worried about coming in." "My friend said I shouldn't." Do not brush it off with a reassuring platitude. Hold the moment briefly:
“That's completely understandable — most of our patients felt exactly that way before their first visit. You're in good hands. The doctor takes her time, there's no pressure on anything today, and you can stop at any point and ask anything you like.”
INNER STANCE  You are not a counsellor or a therapist. You are not trying to solve her nervousness. You are simply telling her: this is normal, you are not the only one, and we know how to take care of you. That is enough — the doctor will do the rest.
7.  The Companion  —  The Mother, the Husband, the Friend
Patients often arrive with someone. A mother. A husband. A sister. A friend. This companion has their own emotional state — sometimes protective, sometimes skeptical, sometimes just bored, occasionally hostile. Your job is to make them feel welcome too, without making them more important than the patient.
What you say
“Welcome. Will you be coming in for the consultation, or would you like to wait here? We have water, tea, and Wi-Fi — please make yourself comfortable. The consultation usually takes about 30 to 40 minutes.”
If the companion is the decision-maker
Sometimes the husband or mother is clearly the one holding the purse. Be respectful, but do not address them over the patient. The patient is who is being treated; the companion is supporting. Keep your eyes and voice oriented on the patient, and include the companion warmly without making them central.
AVOID  Do not ignore the companion — it will be read as rudeness. Do not over-address the companion — the patient will feel diminished. Do not let the companion fill out the patient's form. Do not discuss costs or treatments with the companion if the patient steps out for a moment — wait until they're back together.
8.  The Post-Treatment Goodbye  —  The Last Impression
She has just finished her treatment. She walks out of the cabin a little disoriented, a little tender, a little vulnerable. She has just paid a meaningful amount of money. She is wondering whether what she just did was worth it. Your face is the answer she gets.
What you say
“All done? You did wonderfully. Here, sit for a moment if you'd like — sip some water. How did it go?”
Let her answer. Sometimes she will say "fine." Sometimes she will share the whole experience. Either is okay — the question itself tells her that we cared what it felt like, not just that she paid the bill.
Walk her out, do not just nod
“Take care, [Name]ji. We'll see you on [date] at [time] for your next session — I've messaged you the details. And please — call us anytime if you have any questions about the aftercare, even small things. That's what we're here for. Have a lovely evening.”
THIRD AFFIRMATION  ·  THE GOODBYE
“Call us anytime, for anything. That's what we're here for.”
THE PSYCHOLOGY  The goodbye is the moment most clinics waste. The patient has paid; the desk's instinct is to move on to the next task. But the goodbye is where she decides, on the walk to her car, whether to tell her sister about this place. The thirty seconds you spend at the door — walking her out, calling her by name, inviting her to call anytime — buys you the next referral. The desk that processes payment and immediately turns away loses that referral and never knows it lost it.
AVOID  Do not say goodbye while typing. Do not call out goodbye to her back as she leaves. Do not say "thank you for your payment." Do not let her open the door herself if you can see it. The patient who leaves through a door you opened tells one more person about us than the patient who leaves through a door she opened.
9.  The Rebooking Moment  —  Without the Pressure
The doctor or counsellor has recommended the next visit. The patient is at your desk to lock the date. This is not a sales moment. This is a logistics moment that needs to feel like care.
What you say
“Doctor has recommended your next session in about three weeks. Let me find a time that works for you. Are weekdays easier or weekends? Morning or evening?”
Offer options. Two slots, three at most. Too many options paralyses; too few feels like a push. "How about Tuesday the 14th at 4 pm, or Saturday the 18th at 11 am — either works?"
If she hesitates
“That's completely fine — take a day to check your calendar. I'll hold the Saturday slot for you until tomorrow evening. Just message me on this number when you've decided, no need to call back. And if neither works, we'll find something that does.”
AVOID  Do not say "you need to come on time or your results will suffer." Do not pressure her if she hesitates. Do not book her without confirming. Do not give her a date you know the doctor is unlikely to honour. Holding the slot loosely for a day produces more confirmed bookings than locking it under pressure.
10.  The Complaint at the Desk  —  When Something Has Gone Wrong
The moment
A patient is standing at your desk, agitated. The complaint may be small — a delay, a confusion about billing, an aftercare instruction she misunderstood. Or it may be serious — a treatment outcome she is unhappy with, a reaction she is worried about. You will not always know which one it is in the first sentence. Treat every complaint as if it is serious until proven otherwise.
What you do first — in this exact order
Stop everything else. Phone goes down. Screen turns away. Other tasks pause.
Look at her, not the form.
Lower your voice. The desk environment around a complaint should be quieter, not louder.
Move her, if possible, to a private corner. Complaints in the open waiting area inflame everyone.
What you say
“I'm so sorry you're feeling this way. Please come and sit — let me understand exactly what happened. Tell me from the beginning, in your own words, and I'll make sure the right person hears this today.”
THE PSYCHOLOGY  The patient who is escalating wants three things, in order: to be heard, to be believed, and to be helped. Most desks attempt to help before the first two are done — they jump to a solution, or to a defence of the clinic, or to a refund offer. The patient stays escalated because she has not yet been heard. Spend the first sixty seconds entirely on listening. Then — and only then — move to action.
What you say at the end of listening
“Thank you for telling me. I want to be honest — I am not the right person to give you the clinical answer, but I am going to make sure the right person speaks to you today, not in two days. Let me speak to our manager / the doctor right now — if you can give me five minutes, I'll come back to you with a clear plan.”
Escalate immediately to the FDM or BM if
She mentions a physical reaction, redness, swelling, anything clinical — the doctor must see her today.
She asks for a refund or to escalate.
She mentions social media, reviews, or legal action.
Her voice is loud enough that other patients can hear.
AVOID  Do not argue. Do not say "that's not our policy." Do not say "that has never happened before." Do not interrupt to defend. Do not promise something you cannot deliver — "I'll make sure the doctor calls you back this evening" is safer than "the doctor will call you in an hour." Do not let a complaint be witnessed by other patients without moving it to a private space.
11.  The Angry Caller  —  Voice Without a Face
A patient is on the line, upset. You cannot read her face; she cannot read yours. Voice is all you have. Tone becomes everything.
What you do
Drop your voice slightly below hers. People match volume — if you go up, she goes up; if you go down, she comes down.
Slow your sentences. Anger feeds on speed; calm slows everything.
Use her name once early in the call, then again at the end. "[Name]ji, I'm so sorry this has happened."
Do not put her on hold without permission. "Can I have just two minutes to find the doctor / manager? I'll come right back to you on this same call."
What you say
“[Name]ji, I am very sorry you are dealing with this. I want to make sure the right person speaks to you about this today. Please give me two minutes — do not hang up — I'm going to bring our manager onto this call right now.”
INNER STANCE  Almost no angry caller is actually angry at you. She is angry at a situation, and you happen to be the voice. Do not take it personally; do not respond to the personal note in her voice with a personal note in yours. Stay warm, stay slow, stay on her side of the problem. The voice on the other end is reading every micro-second of yours.
12.  The Cancellation  —  Keep the Door Open
A patient calls to cancel an appointment. Most desks treat this as a logistics task — update the calendar, end the call. That is the moment of biggest leakage in any clinic. Half the patients who cancel never reschedule. Your job is not to pressure her, but to leave the door wider open than she found it.
What you say
“Of course, [Name]ji — thank you for letting us know. Would you like me to rebook you for another date, or would you prefer to call us when things settle?”
If she has a reason and shares it
Listen. "Travel" is a fine answer; "my mother is unwell" is a serious one. Match the warmth to the reason.
“Oh I'm so sorry to hear about your mother — please take all the time you need. I'll keep a soft note on your file so when you call back, we can pick up exactly where we left off. Sending you good wishes for her recovery.”
If she hesitates about coming back at all
“Of course — there's no pressure at all. If you'd like, I can leave the file open and not call you to follow up. Whenever you're ready, just message us. And if there's anything you want to ask before then — even just a question about your skin — you can call me directly. My name is [your name].”
THE PSYCHOLOGY  The patient who cancels under pressure to rebook never comes back. The patient who is allowed to leave kindly often comes back within weeks — because the only memory she has of GLEUHR is one of being treated like a person, not a slot. The graceful cancellation is one of the highest-leverage moments in the receptionist's week. Treat it that way.
13.  The Phone-and-Floor Juggle
The phone is ringing. A patient is in front of you. A colleague needs a signature. Your screen has frozen. This is the reality of the desk on a busy day. There is a hierarchy.
1.  The patient physically in front of you comes first. Always.
2.  If the phone rings while you are with a patient, acknowledge: "One moment — may I just answer this and put them on a quick hold?"
3.  If you are on the phone and a patient walks in, acknowledge with a wave and a smile. "Sorry, just one moment with this call — please come and sit."
4.  Never let either feel ignored. Both should feel seen, even if only one is being served at this exact second.
If you are truly overloaded, call for help
It is better to flag for the FDM than to keep three patients waiting alone. There is no shame in saying, "the desk is full — can someone help with billing while I greet the new arrival?"
AVOID  Do not let the phone ring while you are processing a payment in silence — acknowledge both. Do not type out a long email while a patient is standing in front of you. Do not make a patient repeat herself because you were not listening.
14.  End of Day  —  How the Last Hour Sets Up the Next Morning
The last patient leaves at 7:30. Lock the door, breathe, then take fifteen minutes to set up tomorrow. The morning you give your colleagues and yourself starts with what you do now.
Reconcile today's bookings against attendance. Note any no-shows or late cancellations — those go to the FDM.
Print or print-mentally tomorrow's appointment list. Mark new patients, returning patients, VIPs.
Clear the desk. Empty cups, papers, anything personal. The desk you leave should be the desk you would want to walk in to tomorrow morning.
Check WhatsApp and email — reply to any patient enquiry that came in after hours, even briefly. "Got your message, [Name]ji — will share full details first thing tomorrow." One line. Five seconds. Closes the loop.
End-of-day note to the FDM — anything unusual today (a complaint, a difficult patient, a doctor running late, a billing issue).
INNER STANCE  The receptionist who leaves the desk thinking about the day she just had makes the next morning harder. The receptionist who leaves it set up for tomorrow makes every morning easier — for herself, for the doctor walking in, for the patient walking in. Closing the day well is half of opening the next one well.
15.  Communication Rules  —  The Receptionist's Code
Always
Look up before speaking. Eye contact comes before words.
Use the patient's name. Twice a visit, minimum — once on arrival, once on departure.
Stand briefly for first-time patients and elderly patients.
Offer water before she has to ask.
Walk her out, or at least to the door, if you can.
Acknowledge the wait — every time it crosses ten minutes.
Thank her at the end. Not for the payment. For coming in.
Never
Never eat at the desk.
Never have your phone on the desk in personal use.
Never gossip with a colleague within earshot of the waiting area.
Never discuss one patient's case in front of another patient.
Never roll your eyes, sigh, or visibly react when a patient is being difficult.
Never let a complaint be witnessed in the open waiting area — move it to privacy.
Never let a patient leave through a door you could have opened for her.
16.  The Goal of the Reception  —  In Order of Importance
1.  Welcome
Every patient should feel, within five seconds of walking in, that someone was glad to see her. This is the upstream variable for every other thing.
2.  Calm
Whatever is happening behind the scenes, the waiting area should feel like the calmest room in her day.
3.  Accuracy
Forms filled. Appointments correct. Payments clean. Files complete. The patient should never be the one who notices a mistake.
4.  Continuity
The patient should leave feeling that we will remember her when she comes back. That requires notes, files, and a desk that operates as if memory is the most basic form of respect.
5.  Loyalty
She should leave wanting to come back, and wanting to bring her friend. This is built across every moment of this playbook — but it is sealed in the goodbye.
17.  Quick Reference Card
Print this page. Keep it inside your desk drawer. Glance at it before the first patient walks in each morning.
THE THREE AFFIRMATIONS  ·  TIMING
“Welcome:  “Welcome to GLEUHR. Please come in.”    ·    The Wait:  “Thank you for your patience. She'll be with you in just a few minutes.”    ·    The Goodbye:  “Call us anytime, for anything. That's what we're here for.””

THE INNER STANCE  ·  RE-READ EVERY MORNING
“You are not a person who runs a desk. You are the first face and the last voice of GLEUHR. Look up. Smile. Use her name. The patient is the most important thing in this room — every patient, every time.”

THE NEVER LIST  Never eat at the desk. Never have your phone in personal use. Never gossip in earshot of waiting patients. Never let a complaint be public. Never let a patient leave through a door you could have opened. Never skip the goodbye.
